subject: business-studies
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: A stakeholder differs from a shareholder in that a stakeholder:
options: Can only be an employee of the business
Receives dividends but has no voting rights
Always owns a share of the company
Is any group or individual with an interest in or affected by the business, not necessarily an owner
questions.explain: Stakeholders include anyone affected by the firm (employees, suppliers, the community), whereas shareholders specifically own equity.

questions.q: Which statement best distinguishes a business 'mission' from its 'objectives'?
options: A mission is a quantified short-term target, while objectives are broad qualitative statements
A mission is legally binding on directors, whereas objectives are optional
A mission sets out the overarching purpose and reason a business exists, while objectives are the specific, measurable goals that flow from it
A mission only applies to charities, whereas objectives only apply to companies
questions.explain: The mission states the firm's fundamental purpose, and SMART objectives are the concrete targets derived from that purpose.

questions.q: Which pair of stakeholder objectives is most likely to conflict in the short term?
options: Managers wanting growth and customers wanting variety
Shareholders seeking higher dividends and employees seeking higher wages
Customers wanting high quality and suppliers wanting prompt payment
The local community wanting jobs and the government wanting tax revenue
questions.explain: Money paid out as higher wages reduces the profit available for dividends, creating a direct shareholder-employee conflict.

questions.q: A joint venture is best described as:
options: A firm splitting into two independent companies
One firm fully acquiring another
A government takeover of a private firm
Two or more firms agreeing to pool resources for a specific project while remaining separate entities
questions.explain: A joint venture lets firms share costs, risks and expertise on a defined project without losing their own identities.

questions.q: A 'divorce of ownership and control' is most associated with:
options: Large public limited companies where shareholders own but salaried managers control the firm
Sole traders
Partnerships of two people
Charities
questions.explain: In large plcs, dispersed shareholders own the firm while professional managers run it, separating ownership from control.

questions.q: Market share is most accurately calculated as:
options: The firm's profit as a percentage of revenue
The firm's sales revenue as a percentage of total market sales revenue
The number of competitors divided by total firms
The firm's sales divided by its total costs
questions.explain: Market share = (a firm's sales / total market sales) x 100, showing its proportion of the whole market.

questions.q: Which of the following is a characteristic of the public sector?
options: Organisations owned and run by private shareholders to maximise profit
Voluntary organisations run by charities and not-for-profits
Organisations owned and funded by the state to provide services such as the NHS
Businesses owned by a single self-employed individual
questions.explain: Public sector organisations are government-owned and aim to provide services rather than maximise profit.

questions.q: The principal difference between a private limited company (Ltd) and a public limited company (plc) is that:
options: A plc can offer its shares for sale to the general public, typically via a stock exchange
Only an Ltd pays corporation tax
A plc cannot pay dividends to shareholders
Only a plc has limited liability
questions.explain: A plc may sell shares to the public on a stock market, whereas an Ltd's shares are sold privately with restrictions on transfer.

questions.q: In a traditional partnership without limited status, the partners:
options: Cannot share profits
Have limited liability for the firm's debts
Share unlimited liability and are jointly responsible for the firm's debts
Must register shares at a stock exchange
questions.explain: Ordinary partners have unlimited liability and are jointly liable for the partnership's debts.

questions.q: Backward vertical integration involves a business merging with or acquiring:
options: A retailer that sells its products
An unrelated business to spread risk
A supplier earlier in its supply chain
A competitor at the same stage of production
questions.explain: Backward vertical integration secures supplies by acquiring a firm earlier in the supply chain.

questions.q: Which is the most likely drawback of a sole trader converting into a public limited company?
options: Loss of limited liability
A legal ban on hiring employees
A risk of losing control as ownership becomes dispersed among many shareholders
Inability to raise capital
questions.explain: Floating shares widens ownership, diluting the founder's control and exposing the firm to takeover.

questions.q: In a takeover, unlike a merger:
options: One firm acquires a controlling interest in another, which may be contested
The acquired firm always remains independently managed
No exchange of shares or cash takes place
Both firms agree to combine as equals to form a new entity
questions.explain: A takeover sees one firm buy a controlling stake in another and is often hostile, unlike an agreed merger of equals.

questions.q: The 'third sector' refers to:
options: Charities, social enterprises and voluntary organisations pursuing social rather than purely profit aims
The tertiary (services) sector of the economy
Government departments providing public services
Multinational corporations operating in three or more countries
questions.explain: The third sector comprises non-governmental, not-for-profit organisations such as charities and social enterprises.

questions.q: An ageing population shifting consumer demand toward healthcare products is an example of which PESTLE factor?
options: Economic
Political
Legal
Social
questions.explain: Demographic and lifestyle changes such as an ageing population are social factors in PESTLE analysis.

questions.q: A profit-maximising objective means the firm aims to:
options: Achieve the greatest possible positive difference between total revenue and total costs
Maximise market share at the expense of profit
Break even as quickly as possible
Maximise sales volume regardless of cost
questions.explain: Profit maximisation seeks the largest gap between total revenue and total cost.

questions.q: An advantage of inorganic (external) growth over organic growth is usually that it:
options: Can achieve rapid expansion and instant market share
Always reduces costs immediately
Carries no financial risk
Never causes culture clashes
questions.explain: Mergers and takeovers deliver fast growth and immediate market share, unlike slower organic expansion.

questions.q: A reason some firms deliberately choose to stay small is that:
options: Small firms always earn higher total profits than large firms
Economies of scale only benefit small firms
Limited liability is only available to small firms
They can offer personalised service and flexibility in a niche the owner wishes to retain control over
questions.explain: Staying small lets owners keep control and serve niches with flexible, personal service that large rivals cannot match.

questions.q: Internal (organic) growth is best described as growth achieved by:
options: Forming a joint venture with an overseas partner
Acquiring a controlling stake in another company
Merging with a competitor of similar size
Expanding the firm's own operations, such as opening new outlets or launching products
questions.explain: Organic growth uses the business's own resources to expand internally rather than combining with another firm.

questions.q: Limited liability primarily protects shareholders by ensuring that:
options: Their personal assets cannot be claimed to pay company debts beyond the amount they invested
They cannot be sued for negligence in any circumstances
The company can never be made bankrupt
They are guaranteed a dividend each year
questions.explain: Limited liability caps a shareholder's loss at their investment, shielding their personal assets from the company's debts.

questions.q: A potential downside of limited liability for those dealing with a small Ltd is that:
options: The company cannot enter contracts
Shareholders risk their personal homes
Creditors may struggle to recover debts if the company fails with few assets
Directors automatically lose their salaries
questions.explain: Because liability is limited to the company's assets, creditors of an insolvent Ltd may not be fully repaid.

questions.q: Which best explains why economic growth in the wider economy might lead a firm to revise its objectives?
options: Rising consumer incomes may raise demand, encouraging more ambitious growth objectives
It forces all firms to become charities
It guarantees the firm will fail
It removes the need for any objectives
questions.explain: A growing economy tends to raise incomes and demand, prompting firms to set more expansionary objectives.

questions.q: Which is the clearest benefit to a business of growing in size?
options: A legal requirement to reduce prices
The ability to exploit economies of scale and lower average costs
Automatic protection from economic recessions
Guaranteed elimination of all competition
questions.explain: A key motive for growth is achieving economies of scale that reduce average unit costs and improve competitiveness.

questions.q: A horizontal merger occurs when a firm combines with:
options: Another firm at the same stage of production in the same industry
A customer further forward in the supply chain
A supplier further back in its supply chain
A firm in a completely unrelated industry
questions.explain: A horizontal merger joins two firms at the same stage of the same industry, e.g. two car manufacturers.

questions.q: Which is a likely cause of diseconomies of scale?
options: Communication and coordination problems as the organisation becomes too large
Spreading research costs over more units
Bulk-buying discounts from suppliers
Access to cheaper finance
questions.explain: As firms grow very large, poor communication and weaker motivation can raise average costs, causing diseconomies of scale.

questions.q: The market size of a product can be measured by:
options: The total value or volume of sales of all firms in that market
A single firm's profit margin
The firm's advertising budget
Only the number of firms competing
questions.explain: Market size is the total sales (by value or volume) of all firms supplying that market.

questions.q: A sole trader business is best characterised by:
options: A minimum of two and a maximum of twenty owners
A requirement to file accounts at Companies House
Limited liability and a separate legal identity
Unlimited liability and the owner being legally inseparable from the business
questions.explain: A sole trader has no separate legal identity, so the owner bears unlimited liability for all business debts.

questions.q: A key implication of incorporation for the owners of a private limited company is that:
options: They must publish full accounts and float shares on a stock exchange
They become personally liable for all the company's debts
The business gains a separate legal identity and shareholders enjoy limited liability
Profits are automatically exempt from corporation tax
questions.explain: Incorporation creates a separate legal entity so the company, not its shareholders, owns assets and owes debts, giving owners limited liability.

questions.q: An entrepreneur is best defined as someone who:
options: Manages a department within an established firm
Bears the risk and organises the factors of production to create a new venture
Audits company accounts independently
Provides loan capital to businesses for interest
questions.explain: Entrepreneurs take on financial risk and combine land, labour and capital to set up and run a business.

questions.q: Which element of PESTLE would the introduction of a new minimum wage law most directly fall under?
options: Economic only
Technological
Social
Legal (and political)
questions.explain: A minimum wage is set through legislation, making it primarily a legal factor (with a political origin).

questions.q: A business pursuing a social objective is most likely to:
options: Aim to benefit the community or environment alongside or above pure profit
Always operate as a public limited company
Ignore stakeholders other than shareholders
Avoid paying any wages
questions.explain: Social objectives prioritise community or environmental benefit, characteristic of social enterprises and ethical firms.
